takeaway: Mesenteric adenitis: a child with a sore throat, pus on the tonsils and central abdominal pain; a self-limiting viral inflammation of the mesenteric nodes.

question.text: A 6-year-old boy has vomiting, central abdominal pain, a sore throat, and pus on enlarged tonsils. He is apyrexial, but his mother reports 38°C yesterday. Diagnosis?
question.say: A six-year-old boy has two episodes of vomiting and central abdominal pain. He has a sore throat, and his tonsils are enlarged with pus. He is apyrexial, but his mother reports a temperature of thirty-eight degrees yesterday. What is the diagnosis?

lines.text: A 6-year-old boy with a sore throat and pus on his tonsils.
lines.say: This six-year-old boy has a sore throat and enlarged tonsils, with obvious pus.
He seems apyrexial now, but his mother reports a temperature of thirty-eight degrees yesterday.

lines.text: He vomited and has central abdominal pain.
lines.say: He has vomited twice, and he has central abdominal pain.

lines.text: The swollen mesenteric nodes are the cause.
lines.say: The tonsils talk to the tummy. Swollen mesenteric lymph nodes cause the pain.

lines.text: It is a self-limiting inflammation, frequently caused by a virus.
lines.say: This is a self-limiting inflammatory process, frequently caused by a viral pathogen.

lines.text: Remember: a sore throat with central abdominal pain in a child is mesenteric adenitis.
lines.say: Remember: a sore throat with central abdominal pain in a child suggests mesenteric adenitis.
